newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Sydney told to get Green Olympics right.
newsitem.headline: Sydney told to get Green Olympics right.

text.p: Sydney was warned on Thursday that if it failed to deliver a "Green" Olympics in 2000 it could end the International Olympic Committee's support for environmentally-sensitive Games and damage the green movement.

Earth Council chairman Maurice Strong, the man behind the 1992 United Nations Earth Summit in Rio, said the international sporting community was concerned Sydney may have over-committed itself in promising the greenest Games in Olympic history.

"There are a lot of people in the sporting movement who are quite concerned that Sydney has taken commitments beyond what you would normally expect," Strong said. "Therefore, if it doesn't work it could set back the environmental movement."

"If Sydney were to get serious egg on its face because of its very strong environmental commitment...that might frighten off the International Olympic Committee or those organising future Games. They may step back from the environment."
In delivering the first of his three environment reports on the Sydney Olympic site, Strong praised organisers for taking "impressive steps" towards an environmentally sound Games.
His report highlighted the use of energy-saving technology, the elimination of leaded fuels, the containment of hazardous waste and the protection of the biodiversity of the site.
Energy-efficient features of the Olympic site are estimated to reduce greenhouse gas emmissions by 10,000 tonnes a year.
The Olympic stadium has two 500 kilowatt gas-fuelled engines to produce hot water and power, cutting annual carbon dioxide emissions by 500 tonnes compared with conventional electricity.

The Olympic Village will use photovoltaic solar panels to generate an annual one million kilowatt hours from sunlight, which with gas-boosted solar heaters and its northerly aspect will cut greenhouse gas emissions by 50 percent.

However, the report criticised the use of PVC (polyvinyl chloride) plastic piping on the Olympic site and the poor relationship between the Olympic Co-ordination Authority (OCA), which is building the site, and environmental groups.

"The OCA's interaction with envrinomental groups...has not developed into the type of constructive relationship that was achieved by similar parties in Lillehammer and which most had hoped for in Sydney," the report found.
In fact, green groups have said their relationship with Olympic organisers is at an all-time low and on Thursday labelled Strong's report "soft".

"Our view is that the Sydney Olympics have a long way to go before the government can claim significant environmental benefits for Sydney," said Jeff Angel, chairman of Green Games Watch 2000, a government-backed environmental watchdog.

The Homebush Bay area on which the Olympic site is located was used as a toxic waste dumping ground from 1949 to 1976. Greenpeace says the Bay is the "dioxin capital of the world" after finding 50 rusting drums of dioxin on the shoreline in June and claims dioxin is buried in 17 known sites in the area.
A report by international environmental consultancy CH2M-Hill, released by the OCA, said the deadly toxic waste dioxin is buried in 12 locations on the Olympic site.
The CH2M-Hill report concluded that as the dioxin was buried under tonnes of soil it now posed no danger to athletes -- despite two sites containing dioxin at twice safe levels.
However, the report also warned that a lack of proper records meant the full extent of toxic waste was unknown at Homebush Bay.
